reading.title: Seeing and Hearing in Word Roots
reading.purpose: Explore how the Latin roots vis and aud connect words about sight, sound, and shows.
paras: Two short Latin roots appear all around your home and school. The root vis means "to see," and the root aud means "to hear." Knowing both roots makes big words easy to break apart.

Look at the vis family first. Your vision is your ability to see clearly. When fog lifts, distant hills become visible again. A baseball cap has a visor, a curved brim that shades your eyes so bright sun will not glare. When you visit a cousin, you travel to see them in person. At home, a television brings moving pictures from far away, and a short video lets you replay a favorite soccer goal.

Now listen to the aud family. Recorded sound, like a podcast or song track, is called audio. A school auditorium is a large hall built so an audience can hear every speaker on stage. Before a spring musical, young singers attend an audition, a short tryout where directors listen to their voices.
Sometimes both roots join in one word. An audiovisual exhibit at a museum uses both moving pictures and clear sound together, helping visitors learn with eyes and ears at the same time.
Next time you spot vis or aud, ask whether the word points to sight, sound, or both.

choices: a large room with rows of seats for a school play
a short tryout where directors listen to performers
a curved brim on a cap that blocks bright sunlight
a recorded video that replays a favorite soccer goal

choices: Museum exhibits are always better when they include loud music and screens.
